title: What an operating system does: processes, memory and devices

videos.script: Ana has just started doing IT support at a small accounting office. Eight people, six Windows computers, one Mac, and a small Linux server in a cupboard. {{office}} On her first morning, three different people tell her their computer is slow. {{slow}} To answer any of them, she needs to know what the computer is doing when nobody is typing. And that is the job of one program, the one that is always running: the operating system. {{job}} It decides which program gets the processor, and for how long. It hands out memory, and makes sure no program reads another one's. It talks to the disk, the screen, the keyboard and the network, so that no program has to. {{does}} Windows, Linux and macOS look nothing alike on the screen. Underneath, they do the same four things, in almost the same way. {{same}} In this lesson you will see those four things on a real machine: processes, the processor's time, memory, and devices. You will watch a program ask the system to open a file. And you will follow a computer from the power button to the login screen. {{see}} Everything in the next sixteen lessons, from installing a system to fixing one that will not start, rests on these ideas. {{title}}
